quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

Checks whether Patrick, about 35, is still with his parent or family in 1880, and whether the household names a mother. Thomas may be dead by then, so a widow's household would support the probate search in item 9. The United States 1880 census collection is name-searchable.

Tests the birthplace conflict. The tree gives Patrick's birth as about 1845 in Ireland, and the 1850 census extraction also reads Ireland, but the objective states Pennsylvania. Family-and-neighbour (FAN) item. Sibling christenings in Schuylkill County naming Thomas Flynn as father would give the same parents, and a sibling's entry can name a mother whose maiden name the other records omit. Search Pennsylvania Births and Christenings for Flynn children with Thomas Flynn as father, and for Flynn godparents who may be kin.

Parents' marriage: a dedicated item for Thomas Flynn and his wife, separate from any child's record. It confirms the couple as a unit, may give the mother's maiden name if this was her first marriage, and its date relative to Patrick's birth corroborates Thomas as father. It does not by itself prove Patrick is their child. Search the name-searchable Pennsylvania County Marriages collection, and check Ireland if no Schuylkill marriage is found, since the couple may have married before emigrating.

Thomas Flynn was born about 1818 (tree fact F3), so his death could fall anywhere from the 1840s to about 1895. A will or administration naming Patrick as a son would be direct parentage evidence. Probate has been held by the Schuylkill County Register of Wills since 1811. The Pennsylvania Probate Records collection is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the county dockets, not a name search.

Fallback for item 9. The Orphans' Court kept estate dockets and distributions, and guardianship or distribution papers may name Patrick and his siblings as heirs even where no will survives. Its records are held by the Schuylkill County Orphans' Court, not the Register of Wills.

items.narrative_markdown: Patrick Flynn appears in the 1850 census in Thomas Flynn's Schuylkill County household. Co-enumeration is indirect evidence that supports but does not prove parentage. Post-1860 censuses, probate, and church records have not yet been searched.

entry.rationale: The 1908 death of Patrick Flynn (tree fact F2, 1908-03-12) already cites a Pennsylvania Death Certificates source (S3), but research.json holds no assertion from it and no parent names are recorded. Pull that certificate and extract the father's and mother's names and the mother's maiden name. The Pennsylvania Death Certificates collection, 1906-1968, is name-searchable, and 1908 falls after statewide civil registration began in 1906. A named father is direct parentage evidence; a named father who does not match Thomas Flynn is a conflict to record.

The parent-child link Thomas Flynn to Patrick Flynn (tree relationship R1) cites a 1860 U.S. Federal Census source (S2), but no 1860 assertion exists in research.json; the only household evidence so far is the 1850 census (dwelling 84). The United States, Census, 1860 collection is name-searchable. Confirm Patrick is listed as son of Thomas in the same household and record his listed age and birthplace. Co-residence supports parentage but does not prove it alone; pair with the death certificate, the parents' marriage and the baptism.

Thomas Flynn (b. about 1818) would be about 52 to 62 in these censuses. The United States, Census, 1870 and 1880 collections are name-searchable. Test whether Thomas or a widow still heads a household with Patrick, and whether a 1880 entry gives Patrick's relationship or his parents' birthplaces. Thomas's lifespan sets the window's reach, not Patrick's.

Dedicated parents' marriage search for Thomas Flynn and his wife, dated before Patrick's birth (about 1845). Pennsylvania Civil Marriages, 1677-1950, Compiled Marriages, 1700-1900, and Church Marriages, 1682-1976 are name-searchable. This supplies the mother's maiden name only if this was her first marriage, so it must be read with item 5. It confirms the couple as a unit and dates their union; it does not by itself prove Patrick is their child. If the marriage took place in Ireland, it falls outside this locality.

Remarriage check. Search Thomas Flynn and any wife's name across the statewide marriage collections (Civil Marriages, Compiled Marriages, County Marriages 1775-1991) for a second or earlier marriage, and for a widow's remarriage after Thomas's death. A surname on one marriage record may be a prior married name, so no finding should treat it as the mother's birth name until this search is run.

The tree gives Patrick's birth as about 1845 in Ireland, while the project objective says Pennsylvania; this item tests which is right. Births and Christenings, 1709-1950 and the Schuylkill County Church Records collection are name-searchable. A Pennsylvania baptism would name both parents. Sacramental registers are held by the parish or diocese, not the county, and Roman Catholic parishes in the county were under the Diocese of Philadelphia. If no baptism exists here, the birth parish is not established by this item.

Will or administration of Thomas Flynn, held by the county Register of Wills (records from 1811). The window runs from Patrick's age to Thomas's likely lifespan (born about 1818, so up to about 85). A will or letters naming Patrick as son is direct evidence. The Pennsylvania Probate Records collections are browse-only image groups, so this is an image browse, not a name search. Patrick's own 1908 estate is not parentage evidence and is not searched here.

Burial records for Thomas Flynn, any wife, and a family plot. Pennsylvania Cemetery Records, ca. 1700-ca. 1950, is name-searchable. Burial entries and inscriptions can give ages, relationships and death years, which can place Patrick within a family and test whether a named wife is his mother. This is a contextual and FAN source, not a direct parentage record on its own.

United States, Mortality Schedules, 1850-1880, is name-searchable. A death in Thomas Flynn's household in these years would name the decedent and the relationship and age of household members. It can show whether a wife or a child died there, and it can name a wife whose maiden name is unknown. Use it to test the household reconstructed from items 2 and 3.

FAN item. Browse the dwellings adjacent to dwelling 84 in the 1850 census (Thomas Flynn's household) for other Flynn households, Irish-born neighbours, and relatives who may share a household. Neighbours and kin in the same enumeration can name a common origin and a sibling or brother-in-law who gives the mother's name. The name search of the 1850 census is already logged (log_001); this item browses the neighbourhood instead.

Thomas Flynn's naturalization declaration (born about 1818 in Ireland). Pennsylvania Eastern and Middle District naturalization records are name-searchable, and the Schuylkill naturalization image group (1849-1915) is browse-only. Its value is the origin town and the year of arrival, which can direct the Irish baptism search. A declaration rarely names children, so this is a lead, not parentage evidence. Ireland has no locality survey yet, so an Irish baptism item is not written here.

items.rationale: The 1908 death of Patrick Flynn (tree fact F2, 1908-03-12) already cites a Pennsylvania Death Certificates source (S3), but research.json holds no assertion from it and no parent names are recorded. Pull that certificate and extract the father's and mother's names and the mother's maiden name. The Pennsylvania Death Certificates collection, 1906-1968, is name-searchable, and 1908 falls after statewide civil registration began in 1906. A named father is direct parentage evidence; a named father who does not match Thomas Flynn is a conflict to record.

The parent-child link Thomas Flynn to Patrick Flynn (tree relationship R1) cites a 1860 U.S. Federal Census source (S2), but no 1860 assertion exists in research.json; the only household evidence so far is the 1850 census (dwelling 84). The United States, Census, 1860 collection is name-searchable. Confirm Patrick is listed as son of Thomas in the same household and record his listed age and birthplace. Co-residence supports parentage but does not prove it alone; pair with the death certificate, the parents' marriage and the baptism.

Thomas Flynn (b. about 1818) would be about 52 to 62 in these censuses. The United States, Census, 1870 and 1880 collections are name-searchable. Test whether Thomas or a widow still heads a household with Patrick, and whether a 1880 entry gives Patrick's relationship or his parents' birthplaces. Thomas's lifespan sets the window's reach, not Patrick's.

Dedicated parents' marriage search for Thomas Flynn and his wife, dated before Patrick's birth (about 1845). Pennsylvania Civil Marriages, 1677-1950, Compiled Marriages, 1700-1900, and Church Marriages, 1682-1976 are name-searchable. This supplies the mother's maiden name only if this was her first marriage, so it must be read with item 5. It confirms the couple as a unit and dates their union; it does not by itself prove Patrick is their child. If the marriage took place in Ireland, it falls outside this locality.

Remarriage check. Search Thomas Flynn and any wife's name across the statewide marriage collections (Civil Marriages, Compiled Marriages, County Marriages 1775-1991) for a second or earlier marriage, and for a widow's remarriage after Thomas's death. A surname on one marriage record may be a prior married name, so no finding should treat it as the mother's birth name until this search is run.

The tree gives Patrick's birth as about 1845 in Ireland, while the project objective says Pennsylvania; this item tests which is right. Births and Christenings, 1709-1950 and the Schuylkill County Church Records collection are name-searchable. A Pennsylvania baptism would name both parents. Sacramental registers are held by the parish or diocese, not the county, and Roman Catholic parishes in the county were under the Diocese of Philadelphia. If no baptism exists here, the birth parish is not established by this item.

Will or administration of Thomas Flynn, held by the county Register of Wills (records from 1811). The window runs from Patrick's age to Thomas's likely lifespan (born about 1818, so up to about 85). A will or letters naming Patrick as son is direct evidence. The Pennsylvania Probate Records collections are browse-only image groups, so this is an image browse, not a name search. Patrick's own 1908 estate is not parentage evidence and is not searched here.

Burial records for Thomas Flynn, any wife, and a family plot. Pennsylvania Cemetery Records, ca. 1700-ca. 1950, is name-searchable. Burial entries and inscriptions can give ages, relationships and death years, which can place Patrick within a family and test whether a named wife is his mother. This is a contextual and FAN source, not a direct parentage record on its own.

United States, Mortality Schedules, 1850-1880, is name-searchable. A death in Thomas Flynn's household in these years would name the decedent and the relationship and age of household members. It can show whether a wife or a child died there, and it can name a wife whose maiden name is unknown. Use it to test the household reconstructed from items 2 and 3.

FAN item. Browse the dwellings adjacent to dwelling 84 in the 1850 census (Thomas Flynn's household) for other Flynn households, Irish-born neighbours, and relatives who may share a household. Neighbours and kin in the same enumeration can name a common origin and a sibling or brother-in-law who gives the mother's name. The name search of the 1850 census is already logged (log_001); this item browses the neighbourhood instead.

Thomas Flynn's naturalization declaration (born about 1818 in Ireland). Pennsylvania Eastern and Middle District naturalization records are name-searchable, and the Schuylkill naturalization image group (1849-1915) is browse-only. Its value is the origin town and the year of arrival, which can direct the Irish baptism search. A declaration rarely names children, so this is a lead, not parentage evidence. Ireland has no locality survey yet, so an Irish baptism item is not written here.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

entry.rationale: Patrick Flynn's death on 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County is already cited to a Pennsylvania death certificate (tree fact F2, source S3), but no assertion has been extracted from it and the research log holds no search of it. A state certificate from 1906 onward asks for the decedent's father and mother by name, so it is the most direct route to the parents. The index is name-searchable in the Pennsylvania Deaths and Burials collection; the certificate image is held by the Pennsylvania Department of Health.

The 1850 census (searched, log_001) placed Patrick, age 5, in Thomas Flynn's household but gave no relationship field and named no wife. The 1860 federal census, a name-searchable national collection, records each member's relationship to the head, so it can show Patrick as Thomas's son and name the wife. Patrick would be about 15 and Thomas about 42 in 1860.

The 1870 and 1880 federal censuses, both name-searchable national collections, test whether Thomas Flynn's household still holds Patrick and a mother, and whether the wife survived into those years. The 1880 entry also gives each person's birthplace, which can confirm Patrick's Ireland or Pennsylvania birthplace against the tree's Ireland birth fact.

The 1900 federal census, a name-searchable national collection, is the last enumeration before Patrick's death. It gives his birth month and year and the number of children his mother bore, and it may name a parent in the household. This tests the tree's birth estimate against a self-reported date.

A dedicated item for the candidate parents' marriage to each other, searched on Thomas Flynn as groom because the wife's name is not yet known. The county, civil and church marriage collections are name-searchable. A marriage before 1845 would give the mother's maiden name if this was her first marriage, and its date relative to Patrick's birth corroborates Thomas as father. It proves the couple married, not that Patrick is their child, so it needs a companion record that places Patrick with them. Search across Schuylkill and the adjoining counties of Berks and Northampton, since the county was formed in 1811 and the marriage may have taken place in either.

The tree gives Patrick's birth as about 1845 in Ireland, from his age in the 1850 census, while the objective frames him as born in Pennsylvania. A baptism or christening record would settle the birthplace and may name both parents. The Pennsylvania Births and Christenings collection is name-searchable. Catholic sacramental registers are held at the parish or the Archdiocese of Philadelphia, not the county, so a hit here may point to a parish. If the birth was in Ireland, the baptism would sit in an Irish parish register instead.

Family-and-neighbour (FAN) item. The 1850 census search (log_001) recorded Patrick in dwelling 84, family 91, but the researcher did not extract the other members of that household. Browsing the full household for Thomas's wife and other children, and the neighbouring dwellings for other Flynn households, tests whether a mother, sibling or relative lived nearby. Required for a parentage question. The 1850 census is name-searchable for the search itself, but reading the household and neighbours is an image browse.

A will or administration for Thomas Flynn, held by the Schuylkill County Register of Wills from 1811, could name Patrick as a son and the widow by name. The window is sized to Thomas's lifespan, not the research window: born about 1818 and last seen in 1850, he could have died anywhere from 1851 to about 1890. The probate collection in the locality entry is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the estate dockets and indexes.

Fallback for the Register of Wills item. If the county probate images cannot be browsed, the Pennsylvania Wills and Deeds collection is name-searchable and may index a will or deed in which Thomas names his children or the widow. It is a contingency for the item above, not a substitute for it.

Thomas Flynn's burial, and any Flynn family monument, could give his age and sometimes the names of parents or a spouse. Patrick's own burial after 1908 may name his parents on a family stone. The Pennsylvania Cemetery Records collection is name-searchable, and it gives the burial site to check against the county's cemeteries.

The mortality schedules, name-searchable for 1850 to 1880, list each person who died in the year before each census. If Thomas died between June 1849 and May 1880, the schedule gives his age and birthplace, which tests the 1850 age and the tree's Ireland birth. It is a short search that either closes Thomas's death window or narrows it.

Patrick's own estate, filed with the Schuylkill County Register of Wills after his death in March 1908. Heirs and administrators named in the estate file can include siblings and a surviving mother. The window is sized to the settlement period after the death. The probate collection is browse-only, so this is an image browse.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.question: Besides Mary, John, Rebecca, William and Joseph, who were the other children of Thomas Hale (b. about 1810, Pennsylvania; d. 1868, Greene County, Ohio) and his wife Sarah?
items.rationale: Primary research objective. The tree holds the couple and five children; no records have been searched yet for any others.

entry.rationale: The 1850 census lists every member of Thomas Hale's household with age and birthplace, so it is the first place to find children born 1836-1847 who are not in the tree. The US Census 1850 collection is name-searchable (loc_001). Search Thomas Hale and Sarah Hale and read the whole household, including any child under 5 and any grown or boarding child living elsewhere in the county. Allow for name variants (Hail, Hayle; Sarah or Sally).

The 1860 census is the second decennial count of the household and will show children born after 1850 and any child who had left home by 1850. The US Census 1860 collection is name-searchable (loc_001). Compare it with the 1850 household to test whether each child is accounted for, and check for a child who died between the counts.

Thomas Hale died in 1868 (tree fact F2), so the 1870 census should show Sarah as a widow, with any younger children still at home and possibly a grown child in the household. The US Census 1870 collection is name-searchable (loc_001).

The 1840 census names only the head of household and counts the others by age bracket, so it cannot name children, but it fixes the household size while the earliest children were young. The family's arrival date in Greene County is not in the tree, and the tree's Pennsylvania birthplace for Thomas (F1) leaves open a child born there before the move. Search both Ohio and Pennsylvania for Thomas Hale. The US Census 1840 collection is name-searchable (loc_001 nationalCollections).

Baptism entries are the likely route to children born 1830-1856 whose birth dates predate civil birth registration, so they can name a child not yet in the tree. Search the Ohio, Births and Christenings collection (name-searchable, loc_001) and the Ohio, Church and Civil Births and Baptisms collection for Thomas and Sarah Hale as parents, and for any Hale child in Greene County in these years. A baptism naming Thomas and Sarah as parents places the child with the couple directly.

The marriage of Thomas Hale and Sarah bounds the earliest possible birth of a child of the couple, and it may show that Sarah was marrying for the first time. The tree holds no marriage fact for the couple (R1 is an unsourced Couple link). Search Ohio, County Marriages (name-searchable, loc_001) for Thomas Hale and Sarah, and check whether Sarah appears in an earlier marriage record, since a child from an earlier marriage would not be a child of Thomas. Greene County marriage records survive from 1803 (loc_001 quirk).

Thomas Hale died in 1868 (tree fact F2). His estate file, filed after his death, names his heirs and often lists children by name. Greene County probate went to the Greene County Probate Court after 1852 (loc_001 quirk), so search that court's records. The Ohio, Probate Records collection is browse-only (loc_001), so this is an image browse of the 1868-1875 estate files for Thomas Hale, not a name search.

Land deeds for Thomas Hale name his wife Sarah, may carry her dower release, and can name adjoining landowners who are probably kin. This is the fallback for the estate file in item 7: if the estate file cannot be found, a deed of sale or partition after 1868 may name the heirs. The Ohio, Wills and Deeds collection is name-searchable (loc_001 collections).

Thomas Hale's death record or burial entry (1868) may give his age, his birthplace and the names of survivors. The Ohio, Deaths and Burials collection is name-searchable (loc_001). The tree fact F2 gives the death year and place, but no record in the tree supports it, so this item also confirms the death.

Greene County cemetery records and Find a Grave memorials can show Thomas Hale's burial, and family plots often hold the children who died young, which census records miss. Search for Hale burials in Greene County and any stone naming Sarah or a child. Treat memorial entries as leads to check against the original burial record.

A guardianship file after 1868 would name any child still a minor when Thomas died. Joseph, the youngest known child, was born about 1847 and would have reached 21 by about 1868, so the search is for a younger child not yet in the tree, sized to a minor's lifespan rather than the subject's. Guardianship records are filed with the Greene County Probate Court (loc_001 quirk).

If Sarah died in Greene County after her husband, her estate file would name her surviving children as heirs. Her death date is unknown, so the window runs to 1900, sized to a widow's possible lifespan rather than the 1868 death. The Ohio, Probate Records collection is browse-only (loc_001), so this is an image browse of the Greene County Probate Court files.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

Probate of Thomas Flynn, the named father, from the Schuylkill County Register of Wills (in operation since 1811). A will or administration would name Patrick as a son and list heirs, which is direct parentage evidence. The window is sized to Thomas's life (born ~1818; still alive in 1850 and plausibly dead before 1905), not to the 1908 death. The window follows Patrick's death (12 March 1908) and the years an estate is settled. Browse-only Register of Wills image group, so an image browse. Tests the death certificate's claim that Thomas was the father, which rests on a son-in-law's report.

Burial of Thomas Flynn. A burial entry may give a death date and the family plot, which would bracket the probate search. Pennsylvania Cemetery Records, ca. 1700-ca. 1950, is name-searchable, and Pennsylvania Deaths and Burials, 1720-1999, is name-searchable as a second route. Burial records can name a spouse or children buried in the same plot.

Burial of Patrick Flynn after his 12 March 1908 death. The parish burial register and cemetery record may give age, birthplace or parents, which bear on the Ireland versus Pennsylvania conflict. Name-searchable cemetery sources come first, then the parish burial register through the full-text item above.

Delayed birth record for Patrick, if one was filed. Pennsylvania Delayed Birth Records, 1780-1977, is name-searchable. A delayed-birth application is sworn, usually by a parent or a witness, and names the parents, so it could replace the son-in-law's report on the father. It also settles the birthplace conflict if it names a Pennsylvania birth.

This tests how close the informant was to Patrick's family and whether the daughter's record names the grandfather. Mortality schedules, 1850-1880, are name-searchable. A schedule entry for a Thomas Flynn death in the county would give a death year and age, which bounds the probate search, and could show the household's composition in that year. The schedule is a federal return and is not a census enumeration.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

Co-residence with Patrick would support a kin-draw explanation; boarding with unrelated miners would support a labour-recruitment explanation.

The tree already holds Patrick Sheahan's 1875 purchase in Deed Book 42 p. 118 from James Kelly (S1). A brother established on land in the county seven years before Michael's 1882 appearance is the leading candidate explanation, so the deed books must be read for Michael's own purchase, lease or mortgage, and for any instrument joining Michael with Patrick. The Schuylkill deed records 1815-1900 are a browse-only image group (volume 007936752), so browse the deed books by image for 1875-1882 under both names. Per the locality quirks, much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than bought, so company lease records count as well as sales. James Kelly, the grantor, is a FAN lead to note if he appears again.

Church registers are the main residence and kin record for the coal region in these years, since statewide civil birth registration began only in 1906 (locality quirk). The Pennsylvania Births and Christenings collection is name-searchable, and the Schuylkill church register volume (007936751, 1842-1895) is browse-only and includes German-language pages. Catholic sacramental registers are held by the parish under the Diocese of Philadelphia, not the county. Baptisms of Michael's children in 1875-1882 would fix his residence, and sponsors named in the entries are FAN leads.

The 1882 directory (log_002) is the only source so far that places Michael in the county, and it gives no town or employer. United States City and Business Directories (ca. 1749-ca. 1990) is name-searchable. Searching 1870-1885 Schuylkill towns for Michael and Patrick would show the year Michael first appears in the coal region, the town, and whether his listed occupation changed from farmer to miner. That timing bears on whether the move was tied to the 1875 land purchase or came later.

A marriage in Schuylkill, if Michael married there, would show whether he entered the county through a bride's family already in the coal region, which is an alternative motive to mining work. Pennsylvania County Marriages (1775-1991) is name-searchable, and the Schuylkill county marriage volume (007936753, 1870-1910) is browse-only. Locate Michael's marriage, if any, and read the bride's family as FAN leads. No marriage is in the tree, so this item tests whether one exists in the county.

Naturalization papers can state the date and place of arrival and the court that admitted Michael, which bear on whether he came straight to the coal region or moved from elsewhere in the state. Schuylkill naturalizations (volume 007936750, 1849-1915) are browse-only, and Pennsylvania Eastern and Middle District naturalization collections are name-searchable. Confirm which federal district handled Schuylkill cases before relying on one collection. This item is context for the move, not direct evidence of its cause.

Patrick's estate, or any estate in which Michael is named as heir, could state where each brother lived and what property the family held, which would show whether Michael moved to join Patrick. The window runs to 1930 because a sibling's estate can be filed decades after 1882, and Michael's own estate, if any, may fall well after the move. Schuylkill probate volume 007936749 (1851-1930) is browse-only, so browse the index by surname. Probate is a FAN lead for names of co-heirs and creditors.

Michael's death date is not in the tree, so the window is open to the mid-twentieth century.

Local newspapers of the coal region reported mine work, strikes, labour recruitment and personal movements, and could name Michael or Patrick in connection with a job, a lease or a move. No newspaper volume for Schuylkill was returned in the 1875-1885 volume search, and none is named in the localities entry, so first confirm which Schuylkill-area titles exist and where they are held (the state library or a local historical society) before searching. items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.

A year-by-year search for Michael Sheahan from 1876 to 1890 dates his first appearance in the county and shows whether his listed occupation changes from farmer to miner, which tests whether the move came around 1882 and whether it was work-driven.

It should show his county, occupation, birthplace, and any boarders or neighbours. A household of mine workers or boarders would support a work-driven move; a household still working farmland would count against it. Re-read the 1870 household entry for its county before judging the change.

Baptisms of children and marriages in Schuylkill parishes would place the family in the county from a dated entry. The Pennsylvania Births and Christenings and Church Marriages collections are name-searchable. Schuylkill church records are also held as an image group (007936751, 1842-1895, English and German) that must be browsed page by page. Catholic registers stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (archdiocese from 1875), so search the parish registers rather than any county-level index. A child baptised in Schuylkill before 1882 would contradict a move around 1882.

Michael's death or burial entry is the usual route to an occupation and years of residence, since no birth or baptism record for him is in the tree and the birth window is unknown. The Pennsylvania Deaths and Burials collection is name-searchable and the Schuylkill Haven funeral home cards are name-searchable. The window starts at the move and runs to the latest plausible death, since his lifespan after 1882 is not known.

A marriage in Schuylkill County would date his arrival and may name his occupation and home parish. Michael was an adult farmer by 1870, so the window opens well before the move. The Pennsylvania County Marriages collection is name-searchable, and the county marriage image group (007936753, 1870-1910) is browse-only. A marriage made in the farming county before 1882 would show that the move was a later step.

Deed records from 1811 are held by the county Recorder of Deeds. The Schuylkill deed image group (007936752, 1815-1900) is only partly indexed, so browse the 1880-1890 volumes for Michael as grantee, lessee or purchaser. The quirk to note: much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than bought, so a company lease or house-lot lease to Michael would support a work-driven move, and an outright purchase of farmland would count against it.

A will or estate file could name an occupation, a mining employer or a debt to a company store, and it can state where he came from. The Schuylkill probate image group (007936749, 1851-1930) and the Pennsylvania Probate Records collection are browse-only, so browse the county's dockets by image. The window is sized to Michael's lifespan after the move, not to the research window, because his death date is unknown.

His birthplace is unknown in the tree. If he was foreign-born, a naturalization declaration or petition would name his port and date of arrival and sometimes his occupation. The Schuylkill naturalization image group (007936750, 1849-1915) is browse-only, and the federal naturalization collections are name-searchable. Plan this as a check on his origin and arrival, not as a finding that he was an immigrant.

FAN item: the witnesses and sponsors named in the Schuylkill baptism and marriage entries that name Michael's household. Neighbours and kin who moved with him, or who were already miners there, would show whether the move followed kin or a labour recruitment route. Its deliverable is what these associates reveal about Michael's move, not their own facts.

Occupation-specific records would test the mining claim directly: colliery employment or payroll ledgers, and the state mine inspectors' reports for Schuylkill mines, held by the coal companies or the Pennsylvania State Archives. quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

entry.rationale: Track Patrick Flynn as an adult (about 35) and test whether Thomas Flynn (b. about 1818) is in his household. The 1880 schedule is the first federal census to give each person's relationship to the head and the birthplaces of each person's parents, so it can show Thomas as a co-resident father and help settle a conflict: the tree records Patrick's birth as Ireland (about 1845), while the objective and the 1850 and 1860 searches treat him as Pennsylvania-born. The federal census is name-searchable (United States, Census, 1880 national collection). Search Patrick Flynn b. about 1845 and the Flynn surname in Schuylkill County, and examine every Flynn household for Thomas.

Track Patrick Flynn at about 25, when he may still be in his father's household or have set up his own. The 1870 schedule gives birthplace by state or country but not parents' birthplaces, so it bears on the Ireland versus Pennsylvania conflict only at that line. The federal census is name-searchable (United States, Census, 1870 national collection). Search Patrick Flynn b. about 1845 in Schuylkill County, examine each Flynn household for Thomas Flynn b. about 1818, and note whether Thomas is still living. The 1850 and 1860 households were dwellings 84 and 112, so the 1870 household may differ again.

Track Patrick Flynn at about 55, shortly before his death in March 1908. The 1900 schedule gives birth month and year and each person's parents' birthplaces, so it can test the Ireland versus Pennsylvania conflict and whether Thomas Flynn, if living at about 82, is in the household. The federal census is name-searchable (United States, Census, 1900 national collection). Search Patrick Flynn b. about 1845 in Schuylkill County and examine each Flynn household for Thomas, and for a widowed or remarried Patrick whose household names a different head.

FAN item. The death certificate names son-in-law James Brown as informant, so Brown's household in each census (1870, 1880, 1900) may name a Flynn wife, and that wife may be a sister of Patrick. Her household, or a Flynn household next door, could show Thomas as head or co-resident and identify Patrick's siblings. This tests parentage through associates, since Patrick's own household may not name Thomas in every census. The federal census is name-searchable for each of those years.

Dedicated parentage item for the marriage of Thomas Flynn to Patrick's mother. The marriage supplies the mother's maiden name only if it was her first marriage, and the census alone does not name her. Search the county and state marriage collections for Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County and nearby Berks and Northampton counties before 1846, and for any later Thomas Flynn marriage that would make the earlier one a second marriage. The marriage corroborates a father named by derivative evidence (the death certificate); it does not by itself show that Patrick is their child.

Fallback for the 1870 FamilySearch item if its indexed search misses Patrick Flynn or his household, which is common for transcribed surnames such as Flynn. Ancestry's index is a second transcription of the same census, so it may return a different spelling or household listing. This is a paid site: the researcher opens it and captures the results for upload.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

facts.informant_bias_notes: Census enumerator is the recorder, not the informant. The household member who provided the name is unknown. Proximity is 'unknown' rather than 'household_member' because for names specifically, the enumerator may have read a sign, heard a neighbor, or made an assumption — the name fact doesn't necessarily require active reporting the way age/birthplace does.

facts.informant: Unknown household member (likely Thomas Flynn or wife)
facts.informant_bias_notes: Age and birthplace require active reporting by a household member — someone had to tell the enumerator these facts. Proximity is 'household_member' rather than 'unknown' because these facts could only come from someone in the household.

facts.informant: Census enumerator (witness to residence by visiting the dwelling)
facts.informant_bias_notes: For residence facts specifically, the enumerator is a direct witness — they physically visited the dwelling and recorded who lived there. This distinguishes residence from other census facts where the household member is the true informant.

entry.rationale: Question: birth date and place of Margaret Flynn. The tree estimates about 1897 in Schuylkill County, but that birth fact (F4 on I3) cites no source. Statewide civil birth registration did not begin until 1906 (loc_001), so a baptism entry is the likeliest surviving record of an 1897 birth. The Pennsylvania Births and Christenings collection is name-searchable and should name the parents and give the date of birth or baptism. Start here.

loc_001 records that the Schuylkill County Orphans' Court kept registers of births from 1893 to 1905, the only civil birth register before statewide registration in 1906. A register entry would give the exact birth date and the parents. Access is recorded as unknown in loc_001, so first confirm with the Orphans' Court whether these registers can be searched or copied. It follows the baptism search because it may need a written request.

Pennsylvania Delayed Birth Records is name-searchable. A birth not registered when it happened was often recorded later on witness affidavits, which can state the date and parents. This covers a 1897 birth that never reached a baptism register or the county register.

The United States Census, 1900 is name-searchable. Margaret, about three in 1900, should appear in her father Patrick's household in Schuylkill County. The age, month and year of birth, and birthplace were given by a household member, so this is corroboration of the birth date rather than a primary record. It also tests the tree's Schuylkill County birthplace.

Catholic sacramental registers for Schuylkill are held by the parish or the Archdiocese of Philadelphia, not the county (loc_001). The FamilySearch church films for this county, browse-only, end in 1895 and do not reach 1897, so the parish register itself must be asked for. Use this if the indexed baptism search in the first item finds nothing for Margaret.

If Margaret died young, her death or burial entry would state her age, which gives a birth year to test against the tree's 1897 estimate. Pennsylvania Cemetery Records and the Pennsylvania Deaths and Burials collection are both name-searchable. Schuylkill funeral home obituary cards (1914-2007) are name-searchable and can state a birthplace.

Margaret's marriage record, if she married in her late teens or twenties, would give her age and birthplace. Pennsylvania County Marriages is name-searchable and covers the period. This is a route to age, not to the birth record itself.

The Schuylkill County Orphans' Court kept marriage records from 1885 (loc_001). This is the fallback if the county marriage search in the previous item finds nothing. Access is unknown, so it may need a written request.

agent_returns.text:
Mode: create (Add-new). Question q_003, "When and where was Margaret Flynn (b. ~1897, Schuylkill County, PA), daughter of Patrick Flynn, born?" had no plan, so I wrote plan pl_002 as active with eight items.

Survey of the tree:
- Margaret (I3) has a birth fact of about 1897 in Schuylkill County, with no source attached. She is linked to Patrick (I1) as his daughter, also unsourced.
- Patrick (I1) has a birth fact of about 1845 in Ireland and a death of 12 March 1908 in Schuylkill County, citing the 1850 census and Pennsylvania death certificates.
- Margaret has no FamilySearch record reference in the tree, so no pending-hints item was planned for her.

Plan items, in order:
1. pli_004, church, FamilySearch, 1896-1898: the Pennsylvania Births and Christenings collection, the likeliest surviving record of an 1897 birth since statewide registration began only in 1906.
2. pli_005, vital record, Schuylkill County courthouse, 1896-1898: the Orphans' Court birth registers for 1893-1905. Access is unknown, so confirm first whether they can be searched or copied.
3. pli_006, vital record, FamilySearch, 1897-1930: the Pennsylvania Delayed Birth Records, for a birth registered late on witness affidavits.
4. pli_007, census, FamilySearch, 1900: the 1900 census for Patrick's Schuylkill household, for corroboration of age and birthplace.
5. pli_008, church, other (parish or Archdiocese of Philadelphia), 1896-1898: the Catholic parish register. This is the fallback for pli_004. The county's browse-only church films end in 1895, so they do not cover 1897.
6. pli_009, cemetery, FamilySearch, 1897-1950: death, burial and funeral-home obituary records, for an age at death if she died young.
7. pli_010, vital record, FamilySearch, 1915-1925: the Pennsylvania County Marriages collection, for an age and birthplace at marriage.
8. pli_011, court, county courthouse, 1915-1925: the Orphans' Court marriage records, the fallback for pli_010.

No FAN item was added, since this is a birth question rather than a parentage one. The tree's 1897 birth date and place remain unsourced until one of these records is found.

---

I set up a plan for finding when and where Margaret Flynn was born. It starts with the parish baptism records, which are the most likely surviving record of a birth in 1897 because Pennsylvania did not require birth certificates until 1906. It then checks the county's own birth registers, the late-registered birth records, and her 1900 census entry in her father's household. Marriage and burial records follow as backups that may state her age or birthplace.

The first search is the indexed Pennsylvania baptism collection, which runs as soon as the researcher says to go ahead.

output.text_response:
Mode: add-new. q_001 had no plan, so a new plan **pl_002** was written as its first active plan. Nothing else was changed.

---

**Survey of what the tree already holds:**
- **Patrick Flynn (I1):** birth about 1845, Ireland (cited to the 1850 census); death 1908-03-12, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (cited to a Pennsylvania death certificate). No parent recorded on his own facts.
- **Thomas Flynn (I2):** birth about 1818, Ireland. No death, marriage, or spouse recorded.
- A ParentChild link (R1) joins Thomas to Patrick, citing the 1850 census, a 1860 census source, and the death certificate. Only the 1850 co-residence is logged as searched; the 1860 citation has no search behind it.
- The objective says Patrick was born in Pennsylvania, but the tree and the census-derived fact say Ireland. The plan treats Ireland as the tree's reading; Pennsylvania-side items test the other reading.
- The 1850 household (dwelling 84) is already logged as found, so no item re-searches it.

---

**Plan pl_002 for q_001 — items in order:**

| # | ID | Search |
|---|-----|--------|
| 1 | pli_004 | Patrick's **1908 state death certificate**, Schuylkill County — may name parents directly |
| 2 | pli_005 | **1860 census**, Schuylkill County — fills the 1851–1860 gap |
| 3 | pli_006 | Thomas Flynn's county **marriage record**, 1835–1850 — to find mother's maiden name |
| 4 | pli_007 | **Catholic parish marriage register** — fallback for pli_006 |
| 5 | pli_008 | **Flynn baptisms** in Schuylkill, 1835–1865 — siblings naming the same parents (FAN) |
| 6 | pli_009 | Thomas's or his wife's **death, burial, or cemetery entries**, 1850–1900 |
| 7 | pli_010 | **Mortality schedules**, 1850–1880 |
| 8 | pli_011 | **Register of Wills / probate**, Thomas's or his widow's estate, 1850–1900 (browse-only) |
| 9 | pli_012 | **Censuses for 1870, 1880, and 1900** |
| 10 | pli_013 | **Neighbour and kin survey** around the 1850 household (FAN) |

---

**Two gaps noted:**
- The **Irish side** (Patrick's birth, and where Thomas and his wife married if not in Pennsylvania) has no locality entry. A locality survey for Ireland is needed before Irish items can be planned.
- The tree has **no FamilySearch ark** for Patrick, so no hints item was added.

---

**Next steps:** The death certificate (pli_004) and the 1860 census (pli_005) are the first two searches to run.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

The 1860 federal census is name-searchable, and the Blount County volume (005154190, from loc_001) is 99% name-indexed. A Wood woman of the right age with a Georgia-born child would name the parents' household. This is a test only: a household match does not show it is Martha's birth family or that M M Wood is her mother.

Alabama State Census, 1866 is name-searchable. Martha would be about seven, so a household naming a Wood woman with a young daughter Martha, or naming the father, carries the item-1 household forward and tests whether it is the same family.

The 1870 federal census is name-searchable. Martha would be about eleven, and a Wood household with a daughter of the right age and Georgia birthplace would show relationships to the head of household. Its date falls before her 1879 marriage to James M Neal.

Smith County marriage volumes 1857-1876 (volume 007255720, loc_002) are 100% name-indexed. Search for any earlier marriage of a bride named M J, Martha, or Mattie Wood under any surname. Finding an earlier marriage would change which surname is her birth name.

Probate estate files (Alabama Probate Records, browse-only with full-text search, not name-indexed) are keyword-searched for a Wood estate naming a daughter Martha or M J as an heir. The date window runs to 1910 because a father of a child born about 1859 could die decades later, and the window is sized to that lifespan, not the 1840-1880 locality period.

Friend and family (FAN) item for the 1869 Lanham marriage: the bondsman and witnesses on the record may be the bride's father or brother (src_002). Smith County marriage volume 1875-1889 (007255721, loc_002) is 100% name-indexed and full-text searchable. A bondsman sharing the Wood surname would point to her birth family.

Hill County probate case files (volume 004820309, loc_002) are full-text searchable but only about 3% name-indexed, so this is a keyword search for a father's estate naming Martha, M J, or Mattie as an heir. Covers the period she lived in Hill County.

Martha's own death or burial entry, dated after her 1888 marriage to Hamby. Texas civil death records start in 1903, so an entry from 1903 onward may name her parents and birthplace. Her birth register is out of reach because Georgia birth records are not in the research set, so this entry is the likely route to her origin.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

entry.jurisdiction: Santa María parish, Vélez-Málaga, Málaga, Andalusia, Spain

Name search of the subject across the general Spanish church collections: Spain, Catholic Church Records, 1307-2005 (name-searchable, very large) and Spain, Baptisms, 1502-1940 (name-searchable), to catch a baptism indexed outside the parish volume. Results are checked against Vélez-Málaga to exclude same-name girls elsewhere in Málaga province.

entry.jurisdiction: Santa María parish, Vélez-Málaga, Málaga, Andalusia, Spain
entry.rationale: Full-text co-occurrence search on García and Romero as separate terms, run unscoped across the parish register text (image group 004104131), to find any act naming both surnames: the subject's baptism, or a parent's marriage or burial. The compound surname is the subject's two Spanish surnames; the Spain Naming Customs page confirms the father's surname comes first and the mother's second, so the father is likely García and the mother Romero, which the search does not assume. Covers variant spellings only as the text allows.

Dedicated search for the parents' marriage to each other, kept separate from the subject's baptism. It supplies the mother's maiden name only if this was her first marriage, and it corroborates a father named only indirectly. Searched in Spain, Marriages, 1565-1950 (name-searchable) by the father's surname García and the mother's surname Romero. The Santa María marriage coverage in image group 004104131_001 starts in 1837, so a marriage before 1837 needs the earlier register, which this item does not reach. The marriage alone does not prove the subject is the child.

Companion to the parents' marriage item, to test whether the surname Romero is the mother's birth name or a prior married name. Searches marriage records for a bride surnamed Romero in Vélez-Málaga, to find any earlier marriage of the mother that would change which record names her parents. The subject's surname alone is not assumed to be the mother's maiden name.

entry.jurisdiction: Santa María parish, Vélez-Málaga, Málaga, Andalusia, Spain
entry.rationale: FAN item. Sibling baptisms and sponsors (padrinos) in the same parish: other children born 1835-1855 to a García and Romero couple, and the godparents and witnesses named in the subject's baptism and the parents' marriage. Those associates can name the parents or show the family's residence. Searched by image browse of image group 004104131_001 where the index does not reach it. Required on a parentage question.

Later death records of either parent, which often name the deceased's parents and spouse. Spain, Deaths, 1600-1920 (name-searchable) is the first search; the Santa María death register volume 008216233_005 (Death Records, 1853-1861, browse-only) is the image fallback. Parents' deaths are dated after the birth window because they are the years a parent could have died after the child was born.

Contextual browse of the Vélez-Málaga orphan records (image groups 008216391, 008216392, 1815-1913, browse-only). If the subject or a sibling was orphaned as a child, an orphanage admission usually names the deceased parent and the surviving one. Included in case the parents died before the subject reached adulthood; this item is a contingency and need not be searched first.

The research-plan agent has created plan **pl_001** for question q_001 — *"Who were Bridget Halloran's other children with John Doyle?"* — and has laid out 12 sequenced plan items. Here's a summary of what it found and planned:

**Key context from the project:**
- Bridget Halloran (I1), born ~1838 in Ireland, married John Doyle (her first marriage). Ellen Doyle (I3) is their only identified child so far.
- The 1900 census shows Bridget had **9 children, 2 surviving**, meaning up to 8 children remain unidentified.
- Bridget's second marriage was in 1879 in Schuylkill County, PA.

**The 12-item research plan (pl_001):**
1. **pli_001** – Pennsylvania Births & Christenings, baptisms 1851–1880 (name-searchable)
2. **pli_002** – Catholic parish image browse (fallback for pli_001)
3. **pli_003** – 1860 Schuylkill census household
4. **pli_004** – 1870 Schuylkill census household
5. **pli_005** – John & Bridget's marriage record 1850–1865
6. **pli_006** – 1880 Kearney household (checking for Doyle stepchildren)
7. **pli_007** – Cemetery child burials 1851–1900
8. **pli_008** – Mortality schedules 1850–1880
9. **pli_009** – John Doyle's probate estate (image browse)
10. **pli_010** – Pennsylvania Wills & Deeds (name-searchable fallback)
11. **pli_011** – Bridget Kearney's death record 1900–1930 (may list surviving children)
12. **pli_012** – Ellen Doyle's marriage entry for witnesses/bondsmen (possible siblings)

**Note:** The research-plan agent writes plans but cannot execute searches — that requires the **search-records** agent. To begin execution, you can say "execute the research plan for q_001" and I'll route it to search-records to start working through these items.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1838-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

entry.rationale: Baptisms of John Doyle and Bridget Halloran's children are the most direct list of their offspring. Bridget's 1900 census entry (log_002) reports nine children born with two living, so most missing names should appear here. Pennsylvania Births and Christenings, 1709-1950 is name-searchable. Statewide civil birth registration began only in 1906 (loc_001), so baptism is the main birth record for these years. Search father John Doyle and mother Bridget, with variant spellings of the surname.

Fallback if the indexed baptism search returns nothing. loc_001 notes some anthracite-region church films are browse-only, so browse the image-only Catholic parish sacramental registers serving the towns where the Doyles lived, reading each entry for parents, child and godparents. Diocese of Philadelphia registers are kept at the parish, not the county (loc_001).

A 1860 household with John Doyle, Bridget and their early children would name each child with an age and place them together before the later births. The United States, Census, 1860 collection is name-searchable. Schuylkill was formed in 1811 (loc_001), so the household is in the county as it stood then.

The 1870 household of John Doyle and Bridget, if he was still living, would list the children at home and their ages, which tests the baptism list against a household. The United States, Census, 1870 collection is name-searchable. Check also for Doyle children enumerated in other households, such as with relatives, since the 1900 entry shows only two survived.

The marriage of John Doyle and Bridget Halloran is the parents' own union. It confirms the couple as a unit and dates the start of their children's births. It also records Bridget's maiden name and is the first marriage, since log_001 shows her 1879 marriage to Martin Kearney was her second. Pennsylvania County Marriages, 1775-1991 and Church Marriages, 1682-1976 are name-searchable, and the marriage may sit in either. Its date relative to the first baptism corroborates that the children are theirs.

The 1880 census should show Bridget in the Martin Kearney household, with any surviving Doyle children listed as stepchildren, and may show a Doyle child living elsewhere in the county. The United States, Census, 1880 collection is name-searchable. Search Kearney and Doyle surnames within Schuylkill County.

Child deaths before adulthood are the usual reason only two children survived to 1900. Cemetery burial records name children who died young and often give parents' names. Pennsylvania, Cemetery Records, ca. 1700-ca. 1950 is name-searchable. Search Doyle and Halloran in Schuylkill County cemeteries.

Mortality schedules list deaths in the twelve months before each census, so they can name a child who died in those years and give the age and cause. Pennsylvania, Mortality Schedules, 1850-1880 and the United States Census (Mortality Schedule), 1850-1880 are both name-searchable. Use the surname Doyle and the county, and check the 1870 and 1880 schedules for the years the children were young.

If John Doyle died before Bridget's 1879 remarriage, his estate file with the Schuylkill Register of Wills would name his widow and each child as heirs (loc_001: probate held from 1811). Run this after the census and burial items, which may give his death year. Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994 is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the Schuylkill dockets for John Doyle.

Fallback for the probate browse. If the Register of Wills dockets cannot be reached image by image, search Pennsylvania, Wills and Deeds, ca. 1700s-2017, which is name-searchable, for John Doyle and for deeds or guardianship notes naming his children.

Bridget Kearney's own death record or burial entry, dated after the 1900 census, may name her surviving children by name and give her parents' names. Pennsylvania, Deaths and Burials, 1720-1999 is name-searchable. Search Bridget Kearney, with Halloran as her birth name and Doyle as a prior married name.

Breadth through a relative's record. Ellen Doyle's own marriage, already found (log_003), names John Doyle and Bridget Halloran as her parents. Pull the full entry for witnesses, bondsmen and the residence given, since a sibling may have attended or signed. Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1775-1991 is name-searchable.
