quirks: Statewide death certificates begin 1 January 1911 — no certificate exists for a death in the 1870s-1880s.

County death registers (Kentucky, Deaths and Burials, 1843-1970, collection 1804888) exist for 1852-1910 but 1860s-1870s coverage is partial; many counties have no surviving register for those decades.

For a death before 1911, the primary evidence is probate: administrator bonds (naming the widow or adult son), estate settlements, and probate register entries bracket the death date within months and localize it to the county.
Muhlenberg County probate records survive well for the 1870s and are in Kentucky Probate Records, 1727-1990 (collection 1875188) — browse-only images organized by county and volume.
Church burial registers and cemetery records can also bracket the death.
Census and tax lists establish the last-known-alive date and, combined with the first census without the subject, bracket the death window.

items.question: Using Kentucky death certificates, what were the date and place of death of Elijah Wilkins (b. c. 1814, Muhlenberg County, Kentucky)?
items.rationale: Primary research objective. The census trail (last residence fact 1870, Muhlenberg County) goes cold after 1870, suggesting a death in the 1870s-1880s — but the question presupposes death certificates, and the survey must establish whether Kentucky certificates even cover that era.

entry.rationale: Review pending FamilySearch hints on ZZWK-EL1 before searching — an attached hint may already answer the question.

Kentucky Deaths, 1911-1967 is name-searchable and is the statewide certificate series. Statewide certificates begin 1 January 1911 (locality guide loc_001), so this search can only test a death after 1910. The subject was born c. 1814 and last resided in Muhlenberg County in 1870, so a post-1910 death would be at age 97 or older. This item excludes that possibility; it cannot place a death in the 1870s-1880s.

Kentucky, Deaths and Burials, 1843-1970 is name-searchable and holds the county death registers for 1852-1910. Per the locality guide (loc_001), register coverage for the 1860s-1870s is partial, so a negative result does not prove no death occurred. Search by name with the 1870 Muhlenberg residence as the anchor, then check any hit against the register page.

Browse the Muhlenberg County death register image group (browse-only, nearly unindexed) for the 1860s-1870s gap that the name-searchable index misses. Read each page for Elijah Wilkins, age near 56 to 96, and for the register's stated cause, date and place. This is the fallback for item 3 because the locality guide flags the register as gappy for these decades.

The Muhlenberg County probate records (administrator bonds and settlements, 1858-1889) are browse-only image records. The locality guide (loc_001) says the 1870s probate survives well and that an administrator bond or estate settlement brackets the death within months and localizes it to the county. Window starts at 1870, the subject's last known residence, and ends at 1889, the collection's coverage end. Browse the volumes for an estate in the name of Elijah Wilkins.

Kentucky Probate Records, 1727-1990 is browse-only and carries the same Muhlenberg county volumes as item 5 under a different collection. This is the fallback for item 5 if the image group cannot be reached or does not hold the estate. Use it to check for a probate file or register entry for Elijah Wilkins between 1870 and 1889.

Muhlenberg County Court Order Books, 1799-1901, are browse-only. The collection runs past the question window, so the item is sized to the collection. Order books record administrator appointments, estate proofs and the court's action on a death. A death entry or appointment can fix the date the court learned of it, and the search can reach an estate whose probate bond is missing from item 5.

Church burial registers and cemetery records can bracket the death, per the locality guide (loc_001). Search Muhlenberg County churches and cemeteries for an Elijah Wilkins burial between 1870 and 1911. A burial entry can give the date and the place of death, and a cemetery marker can name a death year.

The 1880 federal census is the first enumeration after the subject's last known residence in 1870. Its absence of Elijah Wilkins from a Muhlenberg household, or a widow or household recorded with a death note, helps bracket the death window between 1870 and 1880. Search by name and by 1870 neighbours.

Friends-and-neighbours item for identity: the sureties on any Elijah Wilkins administrator bond, and the appraisers and purchasers named in the same estate papers, are neighbours and kin who can confirm that the decedent was the Muhlenberg man born c. 1814. Read the bonds in the item 5 image group for these names, and match them to the 1870 Muhlenberg residence.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Although Mexicans use two surnames, most indexed records carry only the first (paternal) surname — search with the paternal surname alone; when the person is not found, search through the parents (a parent search with each parent's first surname, leaving out the child's name). A baptism entry usually names both parents and the mother's maiden surname, the strongest single route to the parents. The Jalisco Catholic church collection is name-searchable and spans 1895. Per the locality quirk, most indexed entries carry only the paternal surname, so search Hernandez with the given name Maria Guadalupe; if not found, search by each parent's surname without the child's name. The surnames come only from the subject's own name in the tree, an unverified starting point (BCG Standard 11): they are search keys, not established names of the parents.

It is searched if the Jalisco baptism search returns nothing for the subject, since the national index may carry a parish entry the state collection misses. Same search keys and caveat as item 1.

Search both the Catholic marriage register and the Jalisco civil marriage records, which the locality covers.

Companion test for item 4: search the Jalisco civil marriage records for a bride surnamed Ramirez with any groom, 1880-1895. If the mother married earlier than the Hernandez union, that earlier marriage gives a different maiden surname or a different husband, and item 4 must not be read as her first marriage. Search the Jalisco Catholic baptisms for children with the surname Hernandez whose mother is recorded as a Ramirez, in 1885-1910, and read each entry's parents. This also tests whether the surnames appear as a consistent household.

Death records of the candidate parents, which often name the deceased's parents and surviving children. ## Hamre prestegjeld, Hordaland, Norway - 1765-1800

Norwegian name spellings were set by the recorder and vary between records (the wiki's example: the given name Sivert written as Syver, Sjur, Siver, Sifuer or Siffuer) — search given-name spelling variants, not just the tree's spelling, before concluding a nil. entry.rationale: Primary search: the marriage register of the Hamre kirkebøker, which holds the Meland sokn (including the farm Hestdal) per the loc_001 locality entry, in the collection Norway, Marriages, 1660-1926 (name-searchable). Unna was born May 1745, so a first marriage most plausibly falls about 1763-1800. Search her as Unna Halsteinsdatter and under spelling variants of the given name and patronymic, since the recorder set spellings; do not conclude a nil before the variants are tried. Record every marriage of Unna found, not only the first, because a remarriage cannot be excluded until all her entries are seen. The entry should name the groom and the marriage date.

Fallback for item 1: if the name-searchable marriage collection gives no Unna entry, browse the page images of the Hamre kirkebøker marriage volumes for 1763-1800 and read the entries by hand, since Norwegian indexing is incomplete and spellings vary. The volume search for this place returned no image groups, so confirm the volume list through the FamilySearch Catalog before browsing.

Identity anchor: the baptism of Unna in the Hamre kirkebøker (Norway Baptisms, 1634-1927, name-searchable), which should name her father, so that the patronymic Halsteinsdatter is tied to a named father and the household can be followed into the marriage search. items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1840-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1840-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

**Mode:** Create. No plan existed for this question. The subject is the project's own subject (I1), so I planned from the tree without a FamilySearch profile lookup.

**Tree survey:** Josiah is recorded with a birth about 1828 in Ohio (F1), a military service fact dated 1862–1865 with an Indiana standard place (F2), and a death in 1879 in Vigo County, Indiana (F3). The tree has no relationships and no sources. Nothing in the tree places him between 1850 and 1865 except the 1862 service, which carries no residence.

**Plan items in execution order:**
1. **pli_001, census 1850, United States (Vigo County first):** name-searchable. Household rosters give age and birthplace but no relationships, so co-residents must be matched by age, birthplace and occupation.
2. **pli_002, census 1860, United States:** name-searchable. Shows whether he was still in the 1850 household or had his own.
3. **pli_003, military, Indiana, 1862–1934:** the Civil War pension files are name-searchable. Applications often state residence, wife and children.
4. **pli_004, military, Indiana, 1864–1865:** Indiana Military Discharges, name-searchable. Gives a second residence record independent of the pension file.
5. **pli_005, Vigo County, 1850–1865:** Indiana Voter Registers, name-searchable. Could place him by precinct or township.
6. **pli_006, marriage, Vigo County, 1850–1865:** Indiana Marriages (1811–2019), name-searchable. Would give residence and his bride, a likely co-resident.
7. **pli_007, marriage original, Vigo County clerk:** fallback for pli_006. The Vigo marriage register is not indexed in a collection the locality guide surfaced, so the original is read from the county clerk if the index misses him.
8. **pli_008, directories, Terre Haute, 1850–1865:** name-searchable city directories to place him between census years.
9. **pli_009, probate, Vigo County, 1850–1865:** county clerk. Probate files of household heads or relatives may name him as legatee, guardian or witness.

**Warnings:** The write returned validation warnings that the Vigo County and Indiana items fall outside the "United States" locality. The locality entry is keyed to the country and names Vigo County as its forPlace, so these are advisory and the items were written.

---
Next, run the census items (pli_001 and pli_002) with search-records, then the other items with search-records or search-external-sites as they come up.

items.jurisdiction: United States (Vigo County, Indiana first; Ohio and other states where Josiah may have lived)
items.rationale: Tree records Josiah's birth as about 1828 in Ohio, his 1862 Indiana service and his 1879 death in Vigo County, but nothing places him between those points. The 1850 federal census is the first household record in the window and is name-searchable (United States Census, 1850). Its roster gives each member's age and birthplace and states no relationships (locality quirk), so co-residents must be linked by age, birthplace and occupation. Searched nationally because the locality entry covers only Vigo County and the 1850 residence is unknown.

items.jurisdiction: United States (Vigo County, Indiana first; Ohio and other states where Josiah may have lived)
items.rationale: The 1860 federal census falls inside the window and is name-searchable (United States Census, 1860). It shows whether Josiah was still in the household found in 1850 or had set up his own, and with whom. As with 1850, the roster gives ages and birthplaces but no relationships, so co-residents must be matched on age and birthplace. Searched nationally because the residence is unconfirmed.

items.jurisdiction: Indiana (1862 enlistment; residence at enlistment and later pension application)
items.rationale: Josiah's 1862 Indiana military service is in the tree with no residence attached. A Civil War pension file is name-searchable (United States Civil War and Later Pension Files, 1861-1934) and its applications commonly state the applicant's residence, wife and children, which bears directly on where he lived and with whom after 1862.

Discharge records from the Indiana Military Discharges collection are name-searchable and can record the soldier's residence at discharge, which bounds the window's end. This tests the residence the pension file gives against a second, independent record.

Indiana Voter Registers, 1850-1931 is name-searchable and lists voters by county and precinct. A registration in Vigo County during the window would place Josiah at a specific township or ward and corroborate the census residence.

Indiana Marriages, 1811-2019 is name-searchable. A marriage of Josiah in the window gives his residence and his bride, who would then be a co-resident. Indiana kept no statewide vital registration before 1882, so the county record is the source. Searched first because it is indexed; the original county record is the fallback.

The Vigo County marriage register is not indexed in a collection the locality guide surfaced (locality quirk), so the original register is read from the county clerk when the indexed search in the prior item finds nothing or misses the entry.
City and business directories are name-searchable and can place Josiah at a Terre Haute address or occupation in a given year, which the census cannot do between decennial counts.

Probate files of household heads or relatives named in the 1850 and 1860 census entries may name Josiah as a legatee, guardian, appraiser or witness, which would place him in a household or near a family member. Plan from the county clerk, not a collection id (locality quirk). The date window is sized to the probate creators' lifespans, not Josiah's, so files filed after 1865 are included if they settle a death within the window.

dimensions.name: Correctness
dimensions.rationale: All factual claims are grounded in the tool responses. The tree survey correctly identifies F1 (birth ~1828 Ohio), F2 (military service 1862-1865 Indiana), and F3 (death 1879 Vigo County). The locality quirks are accurately cited: no statewide vital registration before 1882, census rosters state no relationships, and probate/marriage records not indexed in a surfaced collection. Collection titles and IDs referenced in rationales (e.g., 1401638 for 1850 census, 1473181 for 1860 census, 1888129 for pension files, 4112706 for military discharges, 4113739 for voter registers, 1410397 for Indiana Marriages 1811-2019) all match the locality data returned by the tool. No fabricated material detected.

dimensions.name: Completeness
dimensions.rationale: The plan covers the full 1850-1865 window with nine items: both decennial censuses (1850, 1860), pension file (reaching past the window as required), military discharge, voter registers, marriage index, marriage original fallback, city directories, and probate. The question asks both where Josiah resided and with whom — every item's rationale addresses co-residents or household composition. No required element is omitted.

dimensions.name: Tool Arguments
dimensions.rationale: All five MCP tool calls used correct arguments: project_context with the correct projectPath, research_query for questions/q_001, research_query for plans/q_001, tree_query for I1 with includeSources, research_query for localities, and research_append with a well-formed ops array. All calls matched as 'live' with no fixture_not_found errors. No critical argument mismatches observed.

dimensions.name: Record type selection
dimensions.rationale: Each record type is matched to the information need: census (household composition), military/pension (residence at enlistment and post-service), vital_record/marriage (co-resident spouse and residence), other/voter registers (township placement), other/city directories (inter-census residence), and probate (household context via legatee/witness roles). Each rationale explains what specific information the record type provides for the question.

dimensions.name: Objective scope containment
dimensions.rationale: Every item's rationale ties directly to Josiah's residence and co-residents. The marriage item (pli_006/007) explains the bride would be a co-resident — linking the relative's record to the subject's question. The probate item explains Josiah may appear as legatee/witness, placing him in a household. No item pursues a relative's own facts for their own sake; all items serve the question about Josiah's whereabouts and companions.

dimensions.name: Sequencing logic
dimensions.rationale: Sequence is defensible: name-searchable indexed sources (census 1850, 1860) come first; military records follow since they depend on knowing the service fact; voter registers and marriage index come next; the marriage original (pli_007) is correctly marked fallback_for pli_006; city directories and probate come last as supplementary. Date ranges span the full window (1850 through 1865 and beyond for pension). The fallback chain for the marriage item is explicit. No item waits on an identifier only a later item can supply.

dimensions.name: Jurisdiction accuracy
dimensions.rationale: Vigo County, Indiana is correctly identified as the target jurisdiction with a date range of 1818-present, which covers the 1850-1865 window. The plan correctly notes Indiana had no statewide vital registration before 1882, directing marriage searches to county records. The 1850 and 1860 census items are correctly scoped nationally since Josiah's 1850 residence is unknown. No anachronistic jurisdictions are used.

dimensions.name: Plan mode and lifecycle
dimensions.rationale: This is correctly identified as a first plan (no prior plan existed — the plans section had count:0). The skill created pl_001 with status 'active' using an append operation. No prior active plan needed to be superseded. The mode is correct (create/add-new for a first plan), and the lifecycle is properly handled with a single active plan for q_001.
